title: Prompting: writing the job description
hook: Six ways to instruct a model, and which combination gives reliable results.
inPlainWords: A prompt is a job description for the model: who it is, what to do, examples of good work, the shape of the output, and what to do when information is missing.

useCase.title: Turn messy emails into a ticket form
useCase.story: Pull three things out of every email: the order number, the type of problem, and how urgent it is, so a ticket can be created automatically.

approaches.name: Just ask (zero-shot)
approaches.what: One plain request with no examples.
approaches.avoidWhen: You need a consistent format every time.
approaches.example: "What is the order number in this email?"

approaches.name: Clear instructions and a role
approaches.what: Say who the model is, what to do, what to avoid, and what to do when unsure.
approaches.greatWhen: Almost always. It is the base of every good prompt.
approaches.example: "You are a support triager. If the order number is missing, return null."

approaches.name: Show examples (few-shot)
approaches.what: Include two to five examples of input and ideal output.
approaches.avoidWhen: Your examples disagree with each other. The model copies the confusion.
approaches.example: Three sample emails with their correct forms.

approaches.name: Think step by step
approaches.what: Ask the model to reason through steps before it answers.
approaches.avoidWhen: Simple extraction, where it only adds time and cost.
approaches.example: "First list what the customer wants, then choose the urgency."

approaches.name: Structured output
approaches.what: Require a fixed shape that your code can read, such as JSON.

approaches.name: Chain of small prompts
approaches.what: Split a big task into small prompts that each do one job.
approaches.greatWhen: A big task keeps failing in one shot.
approaches.avoidWhen: The task fits comfortably in one prompt.
approaches.example: Step 1 extract the facts. Step 2 draft the reply.

challenge.question: You need the same JSON shape every time, even for strange emails. Which prompt is best?

options.text: "Read this and tell me what's up"
options.why: The output changes every run and cannot be parsed.

options.text: Clear instructions, three examples, a required JSON shape, and "use null if missing"
options.why: It sets the job, shows the target, fixes the shape, and handles missing data.

options.text: Long step-by-step reasoning with no format
options.why: It helps thinking, but does not guarantee a shape your code can read.
Often works, but edge cases such as missing numbers are left to chance.

bestCase.title: Instructions, examples, a fixed output shape, and "null if missing"
bestCase.example: "Order #48213 arrived cracked!! Need replacement before Friday" becomes {"order":"48213","problem":"damaged","urgency":"high"}. An email with no number gives {"order":null}, and the ticket goes to a human.

worstCase.title: A vague prompt with no rule for missing information
worstCase.example: "Tell me about this email" returns a friendly paragraph that differs every run and cannot be parsed. When there is no order number, the model invents one, and a refund goes to the wrong order.

route.travelling: "Order #48213 arrived cracked!! Need replacement before Friday"

steps.label: Prompt template
steps.goes: Instructions, three examples, a required JSON shape, and "null if missing".
steps.goesWrong: The prompt only says "Tell me about this email".

steps.label: Language model
steps.goes: It reads the pieces and fills in the form.

steps.label: Check the shape
steps.goes: Code checks that every field is present and urgency is low, medium or high.

steps.label: Create the ticket
steps.goes: A clean ticket appears in the queue.

takeaway: A prompt is a specification: role, steps, examples, output shape, and what to do when information is missing.
